title: Methods for Characterizing the Co-development of Biofilm and Habitat Heterogeneity
protocol: Set up a double-inlet microfluidic flow cell to grow biofilms.
Create well-defined smooth chemical gradients using the flow cell.
Use P. aeruginosa PAO1-gfp and E. coli DH5α to form biofilms.
Grow P. aeruginosa and E. coli on LB agar plates.
Prepare the flow cell using PDMS bound to a glass coverslip via oxygen plasma treatment.
Ensure the dimensions of the flow cell chamber are 23 mm × 13 mm × 0.24 mm (length × width × depth).
Prepare modified FAB growth medium.
Filter-sterilize the glucose stock solution (pore size = 0.2 μm) before adding it to the FAB medium.
Autoclave the FAB medium with cycle 1 (liquid, 15 min; 121 °C, 17 psi) before use.
Sterilize the flow system by autoclaving the entire flow path using cycle 1, except for the plastic three-way valves located upstream of the flow cell.
Cover all tubing and connector openings with aluminum foil or autoclave bags before autoclaving to avoid contamination during assembly.
Connect the flow system carefully after sterilization.
Transfer a colony of P. aeruginosa or E. coli from LB plates to 3 ml of LB broth.
Shake the culture O/N at 225 rpm and 37 °C.
Dilute the O/N cell cultures in 1 ml sterilized water to a final OD600 = 0.01 as the inoculum.
For mixed-species biofilms, dilute two bacterial cultures to a ratio of 1:1 in 1 ml with an equivalent OD600 = 0.01 for each bacterium.
Inoculate the flow cell by injecting 1 ml of the inoculum to the flow cell inlet from the three-way valve.
Pause the flow for 1 hr after injection to allow bacterial cells to attach to the cover glass.
Resume the flow and pump the growth medium to the flow cell at a constant rate of 0.03 ml/min for each inlet for 3 days.
Observe the 3-day biofilms using confocal microscopy.
Mark the double-inlet flow cell with a grid on the cover glass side.
Dilute 10 μl of green fluorescent nucleic acid stain stock solution (1 mM) in 990 μl sterilized water.
Slowly inject the diluted stain into the flow cell chamber from the upstream three-way valve using a syringe.
Keep the flow cell stagnant and in the dark for 30 min.
Resume the flow to wash out the unbound stain for 15 min.
Perform confocal imaging.
Activate the 488 nm Argon laser for excitation.
Set emission collecting channels for GFP at 500-535 nm.
Set emission collecting channels for nucleic acid stain at 650-750 nm.
Adjust gains and offsets for both channels to ensure bright and clean images.
Select xyz and simultaneous imaging mode.
Use the z-control knob to identify the bottom and top of the biofilm in the field.
Set the z-step to 0.5 μm for acquiring a 3-D image stack.
Use a line average of four for image acquisition.
Image biofilms at three or more longitudinal (x) distances along the flow cell inlet.
Image biofilms at three transverse (y) positions relative to the imposed nutritional gradient.
Dissolve Cy5 in water to a final concentration of 10 mg/ml as a stock solution.
Store the Cy5 stock solution in a -20 °C freezer.
Take a 3-D image stack of the 3-day biofilm with confocal microscopy.
Choose a z-plane with well-separated colonies for imaging.
Dilute 2 μl of the Cy5 stock solution in 998 μl sterilized water to yield an injection solution having a Cy5 concentration of 20 μg/ml.
Stop the pump to pause the flow.
Inject the Cy5 solution into the upstream of the flow cell using a syringe via the 3-way valve.
Close the bubble traps after injecting the Cy5 solution.
Adjust the 3-way valve and restart the pump to deliver the injected Cy5 solution into the flow cell.
Switch confocal imaging mode to xyt.
Activate Cy5 and GFP channels under simultaneous imaging mode.
Adjust confocal settings on Cy5 intensity (laser intensity, gain and offset) to avoid saturating signals.
Choose proper scanning speed and line average to balance the time resolution of imaging and the image quality.
Use a line average of four and a frame rate of 0.15 Hz for this protocol.
Resume flow to deliver Cy5 into the flow cell at a rate of 0.03 ml/min.
Start time-series confocal imaging simultaneously.
Identify the edge of a biofilm cluster.
Generate a distance map for a 2-D section of the cluster.
Average radial patterns of Cy5 intensities to generate a penetration curve.
Import an image set into BioSPA software.
Select proper threshold for GFP and Cy5 channels to create binary images.
Define the edge of a cluster using the GFP channel in BioSPA.
Use the polygon tool to select one biofilm cluster as the region of interest (ROI).
Double-click the selected biofilm cluster to perform diffusion analysis.
Save diffusion analysis results from BioSPA.
Calibrate Cy5 intensity to concentration using a calibration curve.
Dilute fluorescent microbeads in sterilized water to a final solid concentration of 0.2% and a final volume of 0.5 ml.
Vortex the diluted fluorescent microbeads to ensure they are well dispersed.
Inject the diluted fluorescent microbeads into the flow cell following procedures from steps 3.3 to 3.5.
Use a relatively low flow rate for particle tracking (e.g., 0.01 ml/hr).
Switch confocal settings to xyt mode to track particle movement at one z-slice.
Take time-series images with a frame rate of 1 Hz.
Repeat the injection and imaging process at different z locations to generate a 3-D flow field.
Subtract the background fluorescence signal from time-series confocal images using ImageJ.
Open the first image of an image set in ImageJ.
Import the entire image set into ImageJ.
Under Process / Image Calculator, subtract the first image from all subsequent images in the set.
Save the pre-processed image set.
Import time-series confocal images into Streams 2.02.
Select and execute “Identify particles” under “Open process view”.
Set threshold values to identify particles accurately.
Use 0.5 μm as the minimum diameter threshold for particle identification.
Use 5 μm as the maximum diameter threshold for particle identification.
Execute “PTV analysis pipeline” under “Open process view” to generate particle paths.
Check particle paths to ensure they represent accurate movement.
Select and execute “Create velocity field” to generate a flow vector map.
